what.definition: Teaching concepts in software docs means helping users build a correct mental model of how the product works, so they can act correctly even when the manual's steps don't cover their situation.
what.summary: Steps tell users what to click; concepts tell them why. This topic covers why understanding matters (mental models and transfer), techniques for explaining (analogies, worked examples, refutation, diagrams), interactive explanations (simulators, what-ifs, Predict → Observe → Explain), and findings from learning science that make understanding stick.

why.impact: Docs that teach only steps create the Hollow Clicker: users who follow the manual perfectly, then archive confidential data thinking it's deleted, or give a contractor access to every project.
why.summary: No manual can document every situation. Users who understand the idea handle the undocumented cases; users who only know the clicks guess.

categories.analogy: Knowing the bus route by heart: perfect until a road is closed.
categories.description: Procedural knowledge is knowing the steps; it breaks as soon as the user's situation differs from the documented one.
categories.details: A user who has memorised 'Select Share, enter the e-mail, select Send' can share a file exactly as the manual shows. But when the Share button is greyed out, or the person is outside the company, they are stuck: the steps don't say what to do and they have nothing else to reason with. Procedural knowledge is necessary, but it's brittle.
categories.subtitle: Knowing the steps
categories.title: Procedural Knowledge

categories.analogy: Knowing the city map, so you can find a new route when a road is closed.
categories.description: Conceptual knowledge is knowing what the parts are, how they relate and why, which lets users work out steps nobody documented.
categories.details: A user who understands that 'sharing is controlled by the workspace's permission settings, and external sharing is off by default' can reason about the greyed-out button themselves: check the workspace settings, or ask the admin. Conceptual knowledge is the map; procedural knowledge is one route across it.
inScope: What the parts are and how they relate
Why the system behaves as it does
categories.subtitle: Knowing what, how it relates, and why
categories.title: Conceptual Knowledge

categories.analogy: Learning to cook rather than learning one recipe.
categories.description: Transfer is applying what you learned to a new situation; conceptual knowledge is what makes transfer possible.
categories.details: No manual can document every situation: every combination of role, data and setting. Transfer is the real goal of teaching: the user meets a case the docs never showed and still acts correctly. Steps alone rarely transfer; an understood idea does.
inScope: New combinations of roles, data and settings
outOfScope: Repeating the exact example from the manual
categories.subtitle: Using it in a new situation
categories.title: Transfer

categories.analogy: A borrowed map of a similar city: very useful, as long as you mark the streets that are different.
categories.description: An analogy links a new idea to one the user already knows (a workspace is like a shared drive folder), and a good one says where it breaks down.
categories.details: 'A workspace is like a shared drive folder: everyone in it sees what's inside.' The user instantly borrows a whole structure they already understand. But every analogy breaks somewhere, and users will carry the broken part over too. So add the limit: 'Unlike a folder, a workspace also has its own billing and settings.'
outOfScope: Analogies from a world users don't know
categories.primaryFocus: Fast understanding by borrowing a known structure
categories.subtitle: New idea ← familiar idea
categories.title: Analogy (with Its Limits)

categories.analogy: Seeing one goal replayed before hearing the offside rule.
categories.description: Concrete before abstract: start with a worked example (Anna submits a 7,000-baht claim) and state the general rule after it.
categories.details: 'Claims over 5,000 baht go through two approval levels' is abstract. 'Anna submits a 7,000-baht taxi claim. It goes to her manager, Ben, then to Finance, because it's over 5,000 baht' is concrete. Start with the concrete story, then state the rule; the reader now has a hook to hang it on. Worked examples like this are one of the best-researched ways to teach new ideas.
inScope: Named people, real amounts, realistic cases
The rule stated after the example
outOfScope: Rules with no example at all
categories.primaryFocus: Giving abstract rules a concrete hook
categories.subtitle: Worked example, then the rule
categories.title: Concrete Before Abstract

categories.analogy: A sign saying 'This is not the exit', right where everyone thinks it is.
categories.description: Refutation text corrects a misconception by stating the wrong belief, saying clearly that it is wrong, then explaining what is true (archiving is not deleting).
categories.details: Users arrive with wrong beliefs, and simply stating the truth often doesn't replace them. Refutation text names the belief directly: 'You might think archiving deletes a project. It doesn't. Archiving hides the project from lists; you can restore it at any time, and nothing is lost.' Naming the misconception makes the reader notice the conflict and update their model.
categories.primaryFocus: Replacing wrong beliefs, not just adding facts
categories.subtitle: State it · reject it · explain the truth
categories.title: Refutation (Fix the Misconception)

categories.analogy: Learning what a dog is gets easier once someone shows you a wolf and a fox.
categories.description: Non-examples show what the concept is not, which sharpens its boundaries (a draft is not a submitted claim).
categories.details: To learn what a 'submitted claim' is, it helps to see things that look similar but aren't: a saved draft (not sent to anyone), a claim returned for changes (sent back, no longer waiting for approval). Showing the near-misses draws the edge of the concept, which is exactly where users make mistakes.
categories.subtitle: What it is not
categories.title: Non-Examples

categories.analogy: Directions plus a sketch map, instead of directions alone.
categories.description: Dual coding: pairing words with a diagram helps people understand and remember better than words alone.
categories.details: 'An organisation has workspaces; a workspace has projects; permissions set on a workspace flow down to its projects' is hard to hold in your head as a sentence. The same idea as a simple box diagram, with an arrow showing permissions flowing down, plus the sentence, gives the reader two routes into memory. Keep diagrams simple: boxes, arrows, a few labels.
inScope: Simple box-and-arrow diagrams next to the text
outOfScope: Decorative images that don't show the structure

categories.analogy: A mixing desk instead of a recording: turn a knob, hear the difference.
categories.description: Explorable explanations (a term popularised by Bret Victor) let readers change inputs and watch the idea respond, instead of only reading about it.
categories.details: Instead of 'storage cost depends on file count and retention period', give readers two sliders and let them see the cost change. Readers discover the relationship by playing with it. Bret Victor's 2011 essay 'Explorable Explanations' popularised the idea of text that you can play with.
inScope: Sliders, toggles, live numbers inside the explanation
outOfScope: Full working copies of the product
categories.subtitle: Change the inputs, watch the idea respond
categories.title: Explorable Explanations

categories.analogy: A wind tunnel: one model plane, one force, nothing else.
categories.description: A concept simulator isolates one idea, such as a permission simulator where you move a user between groups and see what they can access.
categories.details: Unlike a full training sandbox, a concept simulator strips away everything except the one idea. Drag Anna into the Sales workspace and watch five project icons light up; move her to a single project and only one lights up. The user builds the mental model by manipulating it directly.
inScope: Permission, pricing, routing or scheduling rules
outOfScope: Practising full task steps (see Interactive User Manuals)

categories.analogy: A guided museum tour rather than the whole floor plan at once.
categories.description: A clickable flow diagram lets users step through a process (an approval route) one stage at a time.
categories.details: An approval route drawn as a static diagram shows every box at once. A clickable version reveals one stage at a time: 'Claim submitted → manager approves → over 5,000 baht? → Finance approves → paid', with each stage explaining who acts and what they see. Users follow the idea at their own pace and can go back.
inScope: Approval routes, ticket lifecycles, data flows

categories.description: A what-if scenario asks users to make a decision in a realistic situation and shows the consequence, testing understanding rather than recall.
categories.details: 'A contractor needs to see one project, just for a week. What do you do?' Each choice leads to a consequence: added to the workspace, the contractor sees all five projects. Because the situation is new, users can't answer from memorised steps; they must use the concept. It both teaches and checks understanding.

categories.subtitle: Decide, then see the consequence

terms.detailedDefinition: Don Norman separates the designer's model, the system image (UI + docs) and the user's model, which users build only from the system image.
terms.shortDefinition: A person's inner picture of how a system works.

terms.detailedDefinition: A way of writing that makes readers notice the conflict between their belief and the truth.

terms.detailedDefinition: Working memory holds only a few new items at once (John Sweller's cognitive load theory), so introduce few new concepts at a time.
terms.shortDefinition: How much working memory a task uses.

terms.detailedDefinition: Readers change inputs and watch the idea respond. Popularised by Bret Victor's 2011 essay.
terms.shortDefinition: An explanation you can play with.
terms.whyItMatters: Discovering a relationship beats being told it.

terms.detailedDefinition: A teaching strategy (White & Gunstone) that makes learners notice when their mental model is wrong.
terms.shortDefinition: Predict, see the real outcome, explain the difference.
terms.whyItMatters: A failed prediction is the moment a model can be corrected.

terms.detailedDefinition: Also called the testing effect: quick recall questions beat re-reading.
terms.shortDefinition: Recalling from memory to strengthen it.

challenges.explanation: Correct! Steps are brittle; understanding transfers to situations the manual never showed.
challenges.template: Knowing only the steps is {zone-1} knowledge; knowing how the parts relate is {zone-2} knowledge, which makes {zone-3} possible.

challenges.explanation: Correct! Concrete first, words + picture, and name-and-reject the misconception.
challenges.template: Start with a {zone-1}, add a diagram for {zone-2}, and fix the wrong belief with {zone-3}.

challenges.explanation: Correct! Predict → Observe → Explain makes a wrong model visible, so it can be corrected.
challenges.template: Ask learners to {zone-1} first, let them {zone-2} the real outcome, then {zone-3} the difference.

challenges.explanation: Correct! Recall, spacing and explanatory feedback turn understanding into lasting understanding.
challenges.template: Use {zone-1} instead of re-reading, spread reviews with {zone-2}, and give feedback that says {zone-3}.
